Lecture 18

Convergence in probability, in mean and in distribution; the central limit theorem

Deck B, slides 20 to 30 · 41 min read · 30 practice problems

Solutions stay collapsed until you click them.

Big picture. L17 judged convergence outcome by outcome. This lecture introduces three notions that only look at probabilities or averages at each fixed n:

  • In probability: big deviations become improbable.
  • In r-th mean: the average size of the deviation goes to 0.
  • In distribution: only the CDFs converge; the values themselves need not get close.

It then fits all five modes into one diagram and ends with the most important convergence-in-distribution result of all, the central limit theorem (CLT), and its practical use, the normal approximation.

Part A: the slides

Slide 20/30: Towards convergence in probability

On the slide. Now define Xn​=n1{Un​≤n1​}​ where the {Un​} are i.i.d. uniform. Xn​=n when Un​≤n1​ and Xn​=0 otherwise. What can you say about {Xn​}? Is it true that once an Xn​ is zero, all higher-indexed variables are also zero? No! On every run of the experiment (every sample path), we will have a sequence of zero and non-zero values, where the non-zero values become rarer and rarer but keep happening once in a while. On no sample path would you see convergence to zero, but the occurrence of non-zero values becomes rare. We now characterise this notion of convergence.

Compare with slide 19 (L17). The only change is U→Un​: a fresh, independent uniform for each n. Each Xn​ has exactly the same distribution as before (n with probability n1​, else 0), but the joint behaviour is completely different.

Slide 19: one U Slide 20: independent Un​
A typical sample path 1,2,3,0,0,0,0,… 1,0,0,4,0,0,…,0,37,0,…,0,912,0,…
Once 0, always 0? yes (for u>0) no
Almost sure convergence to 0? yes no
Each Xn​'s distribution n w.p. n1​ the same

Why the non-zero values never stop (making the slide's claim precise). The events En​={Un​≤n1​} are independent, and ∑n​P(En​)=∑n​n1​=∞. By the second Borel–Cantelli lemma (L17, slide 18), with probability 1 infinitely many of them happen. So with probability 1, Xn​=n for infinitely many n, and the sample path does not converge to 0; it is in fact unbounded. ("On no sample path" means "on a set of sample paths of probability 1".)

But they do become rare. The expected number of non-zero values among n=1001,…,106 is ∑n=1001106​n1​≈ln1000≈6.9. Among a million terms, only about 7 are non-zero. For any single large n, Xn​ is almost certainly 0. That is the property the next slide names.

Slide 21/30: Convergence in probability

On the slide. Xn​ converges to X in probability if limn→∞​P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=0 for all ϵ>0. How would you compute P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ) when Xn​,X are continuous or discrete? Example: Xn​=n with probability n1​ and Xn​=0 otherwise. P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=P(Xn​>ϵ)=n1​ when n>ϵ. When n<ϵ, P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=0. Once n>ϵ, limn→∞​P(Xn​>ϵ)=limn1​=0. Xn​ converges to 0 in probability, but not almost surely. a.s. convergence implies convergence in probability.

Xn​p​X⟺for every ϵ>0: n→∞lim​P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=0​

The title's "w.h.p." means with high probability: for large n, Xn​ is within ϵ of X with probability close to 1.

How to compute P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ) (the red question).

  • X a constant c (the usual case). Only the distribution of Xn​ is needed:
P(∣Xn​−c∣>ϵ)=P(Xn​<c−ϵ)+P(Xn​>c+ϵ),

which is a sum of pmf values (discrete) or an integral of the pdf outside [c−ϵ,c+ϵ] (continuous).

  • X random. You need the distribution of the difference Dn​=Xn​−X, and for that the joint distribution of Xn​ and X. A common case is Xn​=X+Yn​, where Dn​=Yn​.
  • When exact computation is hard, bound the probability instead with Markov's or Chebyshev's inequality (see the box after slide 22).

The slide's example. With X=0, ∣Xn​−0∣=Xn​, which is either 0 or n. For n>ϵ, P(Xn​>ϵ)=P(Xn​=n)=n1​→0. So Xn​p​0. This works for both slide 19's and slide 20's sequences, since convergence in probability uses only the distribution of Xn​−X for each n separately. It cannot tell the two sequences apart; almost sure convergence can. That is exactly why "in probability" is a weaker requirement than "almost surely".

a.s. ⇒ in probability (proof). Fix ϵ and let Am​={∣Xn​−X∣<ϵ for all n≥m} as in Theorem 7.6. If Xn​a.s.​X, then P(Am​)→1 (Theorem 7.6). Since Am​⊆{∣Xm​−X∣<ϵ},

P(∣Xm​−X∣<ϵ)≥P(Am​)→1.

So P(∣Xm​−X∣≥ϵ)→0. □ (Bertsekas Problem 15.) Slide 20's sequence shows that the converse is false.

Slide 22/30: Convergence in r-th mean

On the slide. Xn​ converges to X in r-th mean if limn→∞​E[∣Xn​−X∣r]=0. How will you compute E[∣Xn​−X∣r]? When r=2 it is convergence in the mean-squared sense; in addition, if X=0, it implies that the second moments converge to 0. In the convergence in probability example, do we have convergence in mean or mean square? Convergence in r-th mean implies convergence in probability.

Xn​Lr​X⟺n→∞lim​E[∣Xn​−X∣r]=0​(r≥1)

r=1 is convergence in mean, and r=2 is mean-square convergence, written Xn​m.s.​X.

How to compute E[∣Xn​−X∣r]. It is LOTUS applied to the difference: E[∣Dn​∣r]=∑∣d∣rpDn​​(d) or ∫∣d∣rfDn​​(d)dd, with Dn​=Xn​−X. As before, for a constant X=c you only need the law of Xn​. For mean square and a constant, the bias–variance decomposition does it with no integrals:

E[(Xn​−c)2]=Var(Xn​)+(E[Xn​]−c)2​

(Expand Xn​−c=(Xn​−E[Xn​])+(E[Xn​]−c); the cross term has mean 0.) So Xn​m.s.​c exactly when E[Xn​]→c and Var(Xn​)→0. This is the quickest test in practice.

The slide's question: does the example converge in mean? No. E∣Xn​−0∣=n⋅n1​=1 for every n, which does not go to 0. In mean square it is worse: E[Xn2​]=n2⋅n1​=n→∞. So the example converges in probability but not in mean or mean square. (Same diagnosis as slide 19: a rare but huge value.)

Lr⇒ in probability (the red bullet). By Markov's inequality (box below) applied to the non-negative ∣Xn​−X∣r:

P(∣Xn​−X∣≥ϵ)=P(∣Xn​−X∣r≥ϵr)≤ϵrE∣Xn​−X∣r​→0.□

(probabilitycourse Theorem 7.4; last year's HW8 Q7 and Tutorial 7 Q9.) Also, higher means are stronger: if s≥r≥1, Ls convergence implies Lr convergence (probabilitycourse Theorem 7.3). In particular, mean square implies convergence in mean.

The sample mean converges in mean square. E[(μ^​n​−μ)2]=Var(μ^​n​)=nσ2​→0 (L17 slide 15). So μ^​n​m.s.​μ, and therefore μ^​n​p​μ. That last statement is the weak law of large numbers, next.

Toolkit box (Bertsekas 5.1 and 5.2): Markov, Chebyshev and the weak law

These inequalities are not on this year's slides, but they are the standard way to prove convergence in probability, and last year's Tutorial 7 Q8 listed them as tools to "use directly".

Markov's inequality. If X≥0 and a>0,

P(X≥a)≤aE[X]​​

Proof. a1{X≥a}≤X always (if X≥a the left side is a≤X; otherwise it is 0≤X). Take expectations: aP(X≥a)≤E[X]. □

Chebyshev's inequality. If X has mean μ and variance σ2, then for c>0,

P(∣X−μ∣≥c)≤c2σ2​​

Proof. Apply Markov to the non-negative (X−μ)2 with a=c2: P((X−μ)2≥c2)≤c2E[(X−μ)2]​. (This is last year's Tutorial 7 Q8(a).) □

How good are they? (Bertsekas Ex. 5.1, 5.2.) For X∼U[0,4]: Markov gives P(X≥3)≤32​ (exact: 41​); Chebyshev gives P(∣X−2∣≥1)≤14/3​=34​, which says nothing (exact: 21​). For X∼ Exp(1): Chebyshev gives P(X≥c)≤(c−1)21​, while the truth is e−c. They are crude, but they need only a mean (and a variance), which is what makes them useful in proofs.

The weak law of large numbers (WLLN). For i.i.d. Xi​ with mean μ and variance σ2, Chebyshev applied to μ^​n​ gives

P(∣μ^​n​−μ∣≥ϵ)≤nϵ2σ2​n→∞​0,soμ^​n​p​μ​

It is "weak" because it gives convergence in probability, which the SLLN (almost sure) implies. Its advantage is a one-line proof plus an explicit bound for finite n.

Example (Bertsekas 5.5, polling). A fraction p of voters support a candidate; poll n at random, and let Mn​ be the sample fraction. Each reply is Bernoulli(p), with variance p(1−p)≤41​. Chebyshev gives P(∣Mn​−p∣≥ϵ)≤4nϵ21​. For 95% confidence of accuracy ±0.01, you need 4n(0.01)21​≤0.05, so n≥50,000. (The CLT, at the end of this lecture, shows that 9604 is enough.)

Slide 23/30: Weak convergence (in distribution)

On the slide. Xn​ converges to X in distribution if limn→∞​FXn​​(x)=FX​(x) for all continuity points of FX​(⋅). a.s. convergence and convergence in probability imply convergence in distribution. Example: Xn​ is exponential with parameter λn. Then FXn​​(x)=1−e−nλx and FX​(x)=1 for all x [≥0]. Note x=0 is a point of discontinuity, as FX​(0)=1 and FXn​​(0)=0. HW EX2: Xn​ are [independent] Binomial(n,nλ​). It converges in distribution to Poisson(λ).

Xn​d​X⟺FXn​​(x)→FX​(x) at every x where FX​ is continuous​

(Two small slips on the slide: "FX​(x)=1 for all x" means for all x≥0, since FX​(x)=0 for x<0; and the HW's "i.i.d." cannot be meant literally, since the Xn​ have different distributions. It just means Xn​∼ Binomial(n,nλ​).)

What it says, and what it does not. Only the CDFs are compared. The values Xn​(ω) never need to be close to X(ω); the variables need not even be defined on the same Ω. For example, if X∼N(0,1) and Xn​=−X for all n, then FXn​​=FX​ (by symmetry), so Xn​d​X, yet ∣Xn​−X∣=2∣X∣ never shrinks. That is why this mode is called weak convergence.

The slide's example: Exp(λn). As n grows, the mean λn1​ shrinks to 0, so we expect Xn​→0. The CDF of the constant X=0 is the step FX​(x)=1{x≥0}.

  • x<0: FXn​​(x)=0=FX​(x). ✓
  • x>0: FXn​​(x)=1−e−nλx→1=FX​(x). ✓
  • x=0: FXn​​(0)=0 for every n, but FX​(0)=1. ✗

So the CDFs converge everywhere except at the jump of FX​. If the definition demanded convergence at every x, this obvious example would fail, which is why only continuity points are required. (This is the L16 example 1−e−nx, and its non-uniform convergence near 0.)

a.s. and in probability imply in distribution. The slide states it; here is the idea for "in probability ⇒ in distribution". If Xn​≤x then either X≤x+ϵ or ∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ. So FXn​​(x)≤FX​(x+ϵ)+P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ), and similarly FX​(x−ϵ)−P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)≤FXn​​(x). Let n→∞, then ϵ→0; at a continuity point both bounds tend to FX​(x). □

The converse holds when the limit is a constant (last year's Tutorial 8 Q3). If Xn​d​c, then Xn​p​c. Proof: c−ϵ and c+ϵ are continuity points of the step FX​=1{x≥c}, so

P(∣Xn​−c∣>ϵ)≤FXn​​(c−ϵ)+1−FXn​​(c+ϵ)→0+1−1=0.□

For integer-valued variables, compare pmfs (probabilitycourse Theorem 7.1). If all Xn​ and X take values in {0,1,2,…}, then Xn​d​X if and only if P(Xn​=k)→P(X=k) for every k.

For MGFs (the continuity theorem, used without proof by Bertsekas). If MXn​​(s)→MX​(s) for all s in an interval around 0, then Xn​d​X. This is how the CLT is proved.

HW EX2: Binomial(n,nλ​)d​ Poisson(λ), two proofs.

Proof 1 (pmfs, probabilitycourse 7.2.4 Example 3). Fix k. Then

P(Xn​=k)=(kn​)(nλ​)k(1−nλ​)n−k=k!λk​⋅→1nkn(n−1)⋯(n−k+1)​​​⋅→e−λ(1−nλ​)n​​⋅→1(1−nλ​)−k​​ ⟶ k!e−λλk​.

By Theorem 7.1, Xn​d​ Poisson(λ).

Proof 2 (MGFs). Using toolkit fact 9,

MXn​​(t)=(1−nλ​+nλ​et)n=(1+nλ(et−1)​)n⟶eλ(et−1),

the Poisson(λ) MGF.

Meaning. Counting rare events among many independent trials gives a Poisson count. For example, typos on a page, calls in a minute, or decays per second.

Slide 24/30: Summary of the five modes

On the slide. A chart (from Wikipedia): pointwise convergence, limXn​(ω)=X(ω) for every ω; almost sure convergence, limXn​(ω)=X(ω) almost surely; convergence in probability, limP(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=0 for any ϵ>0; mean-square convergence, limE[(Xn​−X)2]=0; convergence in distribution, limFn​(x)=F(x) for any continuity point x.

Mode Definition What it looks at Quick test
Sure Xn​(ω)→X(ω) for all ω every sample path rarely used
Almost sure P(Xn​→X)=1 sample paths, up to probability 0 Borel–Cantelli: ∑n​P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)<∞; or Theorem 7.6; or monotone sequences
In probability P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)→0 one n at a time compute it, or Markov/Chebyshev
Mean square E[(Xn​−X)2]→0 one n at a time, on average E[Xn​]→c and Var(Xn​)→0 (for a constant c)
In distribution FXn​​(x)→FX​(x) at continuity points only the marginal CDFs CDFs, pmfs (integer case), or MGFs

Slide 25/30: Relations between the modes (no proofs)

On the slide. Almost sure convergence ⇒ convergence in probability ⇐ mean-square convergence; convergence in probability ⇒ convergence in distribution. (Link: Wikipedia, proofs of convergence of random variables.)

sure⇒almost sure​↘​in probability⇓in distribution​↙​mean square (L2)⇒L1​

Proofs of every arrow are above: a.s. ⇒ p (slide 21), Lr⇒ p (slide 22), p ⇒ d (slide 23). Here are counterexamples for every arrow that is missing. They are worth memorising, because exam questions of the form "does it converge in mode X? in mode Y?" are built from them.

Claim False because of Details
p ⇒ a.s. slide 20: Xn​=n1{Un​≤n1​}, independent Un​ ∑n1​=∞ and independence: infinitely many non-zeros
p ⇒ m.s. (or L1) slide 21: Xn​=n w.p. n1​ E∣Xn​∣=1
a.s. ⇒ m.s. (or L1) slide 19: Xn​=n1{U≤n1​}, one U converges a.s., but E[Xn​]=1
m.s. ⇒ a.s. independent Xn​∼ Bernoulli(n1​) E[Xn2​]=n1​→0, but infinitely many 1s (L17 B4)
d ⇒ p X∼N(0,1), Xn​=−X; or i.i.d. copies of X same CDFs, values never close

And the one partial converse: d ⇒ p when the limit is a constant.

Slide 26/30: Towards the CLT

On the slide. Recall μ^​n​=nSn​​ where Sn​=∑i=1n​Xi​, and {Xi​} is i.i.d. with mean μ and variance σ2. E[μ^​n​]=μ and var(μ^​n​)=nσ2​. Now consider Yn​=σ/n​μ^​n​−μ​ (centering and scaling). What are the mean and variance of Yn​? E[Yn​]=0 and Var(Yn​)=1. What is FYn​​(⋅)? What is limn→∞​FYn​​(⋅)? Answer: Φ(⋅)=FN(0,1)​(⋅). In other words, Yn​ converges to Y=N(0,1) in distribution.

Standardising. Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation:

Yn​=σ/n​μ^​n​−μ​=σn​Sn​−nμ​,E[Yn​]=σ/n​E[μ^​n​]−μ​=0,Var(Yn​)=σ2/nVar(μ^​n​)​=1.

(The second form multiplies the top and bottom by n.)

Why divide by exactly n​σ​? Look at Sn​−nμ, scaled by different powers of n:

  • Divided by n: nSn​−nμ​=μ^​n​−μ→0 (LLN). Too much shrinking; the limit is the boring constant 0.
  • Not divided at all: Var(Sn​−nμ)=nσ2→∞. It spreads out without limit.
  • Divided by n​: the variance stays at σ2, and the shape settles down.

n​ is the only scaling that "zooms in" on the fluctuations of μ^​n​ around μ at the rate that keeps them visible. The remarkable fact, which the next slide states, is that the limiting shape is always the same.

Slides 27/30 and 28/30: The central limit theorem

On the slide (27). Let {Xn​,n≥0} be i.i.d. random variables, each with mean μ and variance 0<σ2<∞. Let μ^​n​=n∑i=1n​Xi​​ and Yn​=σ/n​μ^​n​−μ​. Then Yn​ converges to N(0,1) in distribution. The Xi​ could be ANY discrete or continuous random variables with finite mean and variance. What is the consequence when E[Xi​]=0 and Var(Xi​)=1? Then Yn​=n​Sn​​, and it converges in distribution to N(0,1). nSn​​ converges almost surely to 0, but n​Sn​​ converges to a random variable N(0,1).

On the slide (28). (Same box.) The CLT gives a way to find the approximate distribution of μ^​n​. For large enough n, we can use the approximation Yn​∼N(0,1). Since Gaussianity is preserved under affine transformations, μ^​n​∼N(μ,nσ2​) [approximately].

σn​Sn​−nμ​d​N(0,1),that is,n→∞lim​P(σn​Sn​−nμ​≤z)=Φ(z) for every z​

(Every z is a continuity point of Φ, so here the convergence holds at all z.)

What is remarkable. The Xi​ can have any distribution with finite variance: Bernoulli, uniform, exponential, a die, a mixture. The shape of their distribution is forgotten in the limit. Only μ and σ2 survive.

The blue question: E[Xi​]=0, Var(Xi​)=1. Then Yn​=n​Sn​​. Compare:

nSn​​a.s.​0  (SLLN),n​Sn​​d​N(0,1)  (CLT).

Dividing by n kills the randomness; dividing by n​ keeps exactly one unit of it. (By the way, n​Sn​​ does not converge in probability to anything; only its distribution settles down.)

Slide 28's practical reading. For large n, treat Yn​ as N(0,1). Undoing the standardisation (an affine map preserves normality):

μ^​n​≈N(μ,nσ2​),Sn​≈N(nμ,nσ2)​

This answers L17 slide 15's question "what is the CDF of μ^​n​?", without knowing the law of the Xi​.

How large is "large enough"? A common rule of thumb is n≥30. It is better when the Xi​ are symmetric (a sum of 12 uniforms is already very close to normal) and worse when they are skewed (Bernoulli with p near 0 or 1, exponential) or heavy-tailed.

Proof sketch via MGFs (Bertsekas Problem 12; L14 Part B, B13; last year's Tutorial 6 Q4). Assume the MGF exists near 0. Let Zi​=σXi​−μ​, so E[Zi​]=0, E[Zi2​]=1, and Yn​=n​1​∑i=1n​Zi​.

  1. Independence turns the sum into a power (L14 slide 6 and the linear rule):
MYn​​(s)=E[en​s​∑Zi​]=[MZ​(n​s​)]n.
  1. Taylor expand near 0, using MZ​(0)=1, MZ′​(0)=E[Z]=0, MZ′′​(0)=E[Z2]=1:
MZ​(u)=1+2u2​+o(u2)⟹MZ​(n​s​)=1+2ns2​+o(n1​).
  1. Take the limit with (1+na​+o(n1​))n→ea:
MYn​​(s)→es2/2,

which is the MGF of N(0,1). 4. Conclude with the continuity theorem (slide 23): MGFs converging to the MGF of N(0,1) gives Yn​d​N(0,1). □

(The same computation with ns​ in place of n​s​ gives Mμ^​n​​(s)→esμ, the MGF of the constant μ: the WLLN, probabilitycourse 7.1.3 Problem 5. The general CLT, without assuming an MGF, uses characteristic functions in the same way.)

Slide 29/30: Example from probabilitycourse.com

On the slide. Assumptions: X1​,X2​,… are i.i.d. Bernoulli(p) and Zn​=np(1−p)​X1​+⋯+Xn​−np​, with p=31​. Plots of the PMFs of Z1​,Z2​,Z3​ and Z30​.

Here μ=p=31​ and σ2=p(1−p)=92​. Sn​∼ Binomial(n,31​), and Zn​=2n/9​Sn​−n/3​ is its standardised version. The values and probabilities behind the pictures:

n values of Zn​ probabilities
1 −0.707, 1.414 32​, 31​
2 −1, 0.5, 2 94​, 94​, 91​
3 −1.225, 0, 1.225, 2.449 278​, 2712​, 276​, 271​
30 2.582k−10​ for k=0,…,30, spaced 0.387 apart (k30​)(31​)k(32​)30−k

How to compute a row (for example n=2): S2​∈{0,1,2} with probabilities (32​)2,2⋅31​⋅32​,(31​)2, and Z2​=2/3S2​−2/3​.

What the pictures show.

  • Every Zn​ has mean 0 and variance 1, by construction.
  • For small n the PMF is lopsided: a tall bar on the left and a long right tail, because p=31​<21​ makes the Bernoulli skewed.
  • By n=30 the bars trace a bell curve. The skew fades like n​1​.
  • The bars themselves get shorter (each value has probability about 0.387×φ(z)), so the PMFs do not converge to anything. It is the CDFs that converge to Φ, which is why the CLT is a statement about convergence in distribution. Equivalently, the histogram scaled to area 1 (bar height divided by the spacing 0.387) approaches the density φ.

Slide 30/30: The normal approximation based on the CLT

On the slide. Let Sn​=X1​+⋯+Xn​ where the Xi​ are i.i.d. with mean μ and variance σ2. If n is large, the CDF of Sn​ can be approximated as P(Sn​<c)≈Φ(z) where z=σn​c−nμ​. (Video link: youtube.com/watch?v=zeJD6dqJ5lo.)

P(Sn​≤c)≈Φ(σn​c−nμ​),P(μ^​n​≤c)≈Φ(σ/n​c−μ​)​

The recipe (probabilitycourse 7.1.2).

  1. Write the quantity as a sum Sn​ (or average) of i.i.d. terms.
  2. Find μ=E[Xi​] and σ2=Var(Xi​), then E[Sn​]=nμ and SD(Sn​)=σn​.
  3. Standardise the boundary: z=σn​c−nμ​.
  4. Read Φ(z) from the table; use 1−Φ(z) for ">" and Φ(z2​)−Φ(z1​) for intervals. Use Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z).

The continuity correction (De Moivre–Laplace). If Sn​ is integer-valued (binomial, Poisson, counts), then P(Sn​<c), P(Sn​≤c) and P(Sn​≤c−1) can be different numbers, but the normal approximation would give them all almost the same value. Fix this by moving the boundary half-way between integers: for integers k≤l,

P(k≤Sn​≤l)≈Φ(σn​l+21​−nμ​)−Φ(σn​k−21​−nμ​).

Think of each integer j as the bar [j−21​,j+21​] in a histogram, and approximate the area of the bars by the area under the normal curve.

Bertsekas Ex. 5.12. S∼ Binomial(36,21​): μS​=18, σS​=3.

  • Exact: P(S≤21)=0.8785.
  • No correction: Φ(321−18​)=Φ(1)=0.8413. Off by 0.04.
  • With correction: Φ(321.5−18​)=Φ(1.17)=0.8783. Off by 0.0002.
  • Even a single value works: P(S=19)≈Φ(319.5−18​)−Φ(318.5−18​)=0.6915−0.5662=0.1253, against the exact (1936​)2−36=0.1251.

Part B: extra worked examples and problems

Convergence in probability and in mean

B1 (Bertsekas Ex. 5.7). Y∼ Exp(1) and Yn​=nY​. (The Yn​ are dependent.) Does Yn​→0 in probability?

Solution

Solution. P(∣Yn​∣≥ϵ)=P(Y≥nϵ)=e−nϵ→0. Yes. (In fact Yn​(ω)=nY(ω)​→0 for every outcome, so it also converges surely.)

B2 (Bertsekas Ex. 5.8; probabilitycourse 7.2.6). Yn​=n2 with probability n1​, else 0. Show Yn​p​0 but E[Yn​]→∞, and no Lr convergence.

Solution

Solution. P(∣Yn​∣≥ϵ)=n1​→0 for n2≥ϵ. But E[Yn​]=nn2​=n→∞, and E[Ynr​]=n2r−1→∞ for every r≥1. (This is Bertsekas's answer to Problem 7(b) below.)

B3 (last year's HW7 Q1; Bertsekas Problem 5). X1​,X2​,… independent U[−1,1]. Show convergence in probability, and find the limit, for: (a) Yn​=nXn​​; (b) Yn​=Xnn​; (c) Yn​=X1​X2​⋯Xn​; (d) Yn​=max{X1​,…,Xn​}.

Solution

Solution. (a) ∣Yn​∣≤n1​, so P(∣Yn​∣≥ϵ)=0 once n>ϵ1​. Limit 0. (b) P(∣Xn​∣n≥ϵ)=P(∣Xn​∣≥ϵ1/n)=1−ϵ1/n→1−1=0 (for 0<ϵ<1), since ∣Xn​∣∼U[0,1]. Limit 0. (c) By independence E∣Yn​∣=∏E∣Xi​∣=2−n. Markov: P(∣Yn​∣≥ϵ)≤ϵ2−n​→0. Limit 0. (d) For 0<ϵ<2: P(∣Yn​−1∣≥ϵ)=P(all Xi​≤1−ϵ)=(22−ϵ​)n→0. Limit 1.

B4 (last year's HW7 Q2). Xi​ i.i.d. with mean μ and variance σ2>0. Let Yi​=31​Xi​+32​Xi+1​ and Mn​=n1​∑i=1n​Yi​. (a) Are the Yi​ independent? (b) Identically distributed? (c) Show Mn​p​μ.

Solution

Solution. (a) No: Yi​ and Yi+1​ both contain Xi+1​; indeed Cov(Yi​,Yi+1​)=32​⋅31​σ2=92​σ2=0. (b) Yes: each Yi​ is the same function of an i.i.d. pair. (c) E[Mn​]=μ. For the variance, Var(Yi​)=(91​+94​)σ2=95​σ2, neighbours have covariance 92​σ2, and others 0:

Var(i=1∑n​Yi​)=n⋅95​σ2+2(n−1)⋅92​σ2=99n−4​σ2,Var(Mn​)=9n2(9n−4)σ2​≤nσ2​.

Chebyshev: P(∣Mn​−μ∣≥ϵ)≤nϵ2σ2​→0. (The WLLN does not need independence, only a variance of the average that goes to 0.)

B5 (last year's HW7 Q3 and HW8 Q5). (a) Xn​∼N(0,n1​): show Xn​p​0. (b) Xn​=X+Yn​ with Yn​∼N(0,n1​) independent of X: show Xn​m.s.​X.

Solution

Solution. (a) Chebyshev: P(∣Xn​∣≥ϵ)≤nϵ21​→0. (b) E[(Xn​−X)2]=E[Yn2​]=n1​→0. Note that nothing about X is needed.

B6 (last year's HW7 Q7). Xn​=X+Yn​ with E[Yn​]=n1​ and Var(Yn​)=nσ2​. Show Xn​p​X.

Solution

Solution. Bias–variance: E[(Xn​−X)2]=E[Yn2​]=nσ2​+n21​→0, so mean square, hence in probability.

B7 (last year's Quiz 2 Q2; HW7 Q5; Tutorial 7 Q8(b)). Xn​ has the Laplace density 2n​e−n∣x∣. Show Xn​p​0.

Solution, three ways.

  • Directly: P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=2∫ϵ∞​2n​e−nxdx=e−nϵ→0.
  • Markov: E∣Xn​∣=n∫0∞​xe−nxdx=n1​, so P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)≤nϵ1​→0.
  • Chebyshev: E[Xn​]=0 (symmetric) and E[Xn2​]=n∫0∞​x2e−nxdx=n22​, so P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)≤n2ϵ22​→0.

B8 (last year's HW8 Q4; probabilitycourse 7.2.6; Tutorial 7 Q4(b); Endsem Q7). (a) Xn​∼U(0,n1​): show Xn​p​0 and Xn​Lr​0. (b) Endsem Q7: Xn​∼U(5−n1​,5+n1​): show Xn​d​5, and compute P(∣Xn​−5∣>ϵ) explicitly.

Solution

Solution. (a) P(Xn​>ϵ)=0 once n1​≤ϵ. And E[Xnr​]=∫01/n​xrndx=(r+1)nr1​→0. (b) Distribution: the limit's CDF is 1{x≥5}, continuous except at 5. For x<5, Fn​(x)=0 once 5−n1​>x; for x>5, Fn​(x)=1 once 5+n1​<x. So Fn​(x)→F(x) at every x=5. (At x=5, Fn​(5)=21​ for all n, which is allowed to disagree.) Probability: the density is 2n​ on an interval of half-width n1​. If n1​≤ϵ, the whole interval lies within ϵ of 5, so the probability is 0. If n1​>ϵ, the part outside (5−ϵ,5+ϵ) has total length 2(n1​−ϵ), so

P(∣Xn​−5∣>ϵ)={1−nϵ0​n<ϵ1​n≥ϵ1​​ n→∞​0.

B9 (last year's HW8 Q1). Independent Xn​∼ Bernoulli(n1​). Does Xn​→0 (a) in mean square, (b) almost surely, (c) in distribution?

Solution

Solution. (a) Yes: E[Xn2​]=n1​→0. (b) No: L17 Part B, B4 (Theorem 7.6, or the second Borel–Cantelli lemma). (c) Yes: m.s. implies p implies d. Directly, FXn​​(x)=1−n1​→1 for 0≤x<1, and the CDFs are 0 for x<0 and 1 for x≥1. This is the "m.s. does not imply a.s." example.

B10 (last year's Tutorial 7 Q1). One uniform U and Xn​=n1{U≤n1​} (L17 slide 19). Does Xn​→0 in (a) distribution, (b) probability, (c) almost surely (can Borel–Cantelli be applied?), (d) mean?

Solution

Solution. (c) Yes, almost surely (slide 19). Borel–Cantelli (Theorem 7.5) cannot be applied, since ∑n​P(Xn​>ϵ)=∑n1​=∞; the conclusion holds anyway (use Theorem 7.6). (b) and (a) follow from (c). (d) No: E∣Xn​∣=1.

B11 (last year's Quiz 2, second set, Q1b): convergence in distribution only. Xn​∼ Exp(n) and Yn​=nXn​. Let Y∼ Exp(1), independent of all Yn​ (and the Yn​ independent). Does Yn​→Y in (a) distribution, (b) probability, (c) almost surely, (d) L1?

Solution

Solution. (a) Yes: FYn​​(y)=P(Xn​≤ny​)=1−e−n⋅y/n=1−e−y. Every Yn​ is exactly Exp(1). (b) No. Condition on Y: P(Yn​>Y+ϵ)=∫0∞​e−(y+ϵ)e−ydy=21​e−ϵ, and the same for Y>Yn​+ϵ. So P(∣Yn​−Y∣>ϵ)=e−ϵ for every n, which does not tend to 0. (c) No: a.s. would imply (b). (Or by Theorem 7.6: P(Am​)=∏n≥m​(1−e−ϵ)=0.) (d) No: Yn​−Y has the Laplace density 21​e−∣z∣ (from (b)), so E∣Yn​−Y∣=1 for every n. This is the cleanest exam-style example that d does not imply p: identical distributions, independent values.

B12 (last year's Tutorial 7 Q3). X∼ Bernoulli(31​) and Xn​=(1+n1​)X. Show Xn​p​X.

Solution

Solution. ∣Xn​−X∣=nX​≤n1​, so P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=0 once n>ϵ1​. (It even converges surely.)

B13 (last year's Tutorial 7 Q10). Xi​ i.i.d. with E[X]=2 and Var(X)=9. Let Yi​=2iXi​​, Tn​=∑i=1n​Yi​ and An​=nTn​​. (a) Means and variances. (b) to (d) Do Yn​, Tn​, An​ converge in probability, and to what?

Solution

Solution. (a) E[Yn​]=2n2​, Var(Yn​)=4n9​. E[Tn​]=2∑i=1n​2−i=2(1−2−n) and Var(Tn​)=9∑i=1n​4−i=3(1−4−n). E[An​]=n2(1−2−n)​ and Var(An​)=n23(1−4−n)​. (b) Yn​→0: mean and variance both go to 0, so mean square, hence in probability. (c) Tn​ does not converge to a constant: its variance tends to 3, not 0. It converges (in mean square, hence in probability) to the random variable T=∑i=1∞​2iXi​​, since E[(T−Tn​)2]=Var(∑i>n​Yi​)+(E∑i>n​Yi​)2=3⋅4−n+4⋅4−n→0. (d) An​→0: mean and variance go to 0. (Note: not to E[X]=2. The Yi​ are not identically distributed, so the LLN does not apply.)

B14 (last year's HW8 Q11). Yi​ i.i.d. with mean μ and variance σ2, and Xn​=n1​(Y1​Y2​+Y2​Y3​+⋯+Yn−1​Yn​+Yn​Y1​). Show Xn​p​μ2.

Solution

Solution. Each product of two independent terms has mean μ2, so E[Xn​]=μ2. Let v=Var(Y1​Y2​)=(σ2+μ2)2−μ4. Neighbouring products share one factor: Cov(Y1​Y2​,Y2​Y3​)=μ2E[Y2]−μ4=μ2σ2. Non-neighbours are independent. For n≥3 the cyclic sum has n terms and n neighbouring pairs, so

Var(Xn​)=n2nv+2nμ2σ2​=nv+2μ2σ2​→0,

and Chebyshev finishes it.

B15 (last year's Tutorial 8 Q2): the "typewriter" sequence. U∼U[0,1]; X1​=1{U∈[0,1]}; X2​,X3​ are the indicators of the two halves; X4​,…,X7​ of the four quarters; and so on. Find the limit in probability, and decide almost sure convergence.

Solution

Solution. In the k-th sweep the intervals have length 2−k, so P(Xn​=1)=2−k→0: Xn​p​0 (and in every Lr, since E[Xnr​]=2−k). But for every u, each sweep covers [0,1], so Xn​(u)=1 once in every sweep, infinitely often. No sample path converges: Xn​→0 almost surely. (Another "m.s. does not imply a.s." example, with no independence.)

B16 (last year's Tutorial 8 Q4). Show μ^​n​→E[X] in mean square.

Solution

Solution. E[(μ^​n​−μ)2]=Var(μ^​n​)=nσ2​→0.

Convergence in distribution

B17 (last year's Tutorial 7 Q2). Xi​ i.i.d. U[0,1] and Yn​=n(1−maxi≤n​Xi​). Show Yn​d​ Exp(1).

Solution

Solution. For 0≤y<n: P(Yn​>y)=P(maxXi​<1−ny​)=(1−ny​)n→e−y. So FYn​​(y)→1−e−y for y≥0 (and both are 0 for y<0).

B18 (last year's Tutorial 7 Q4(a) and Tutorial 8 Q5): discrete to continuous. Yn​ uniform on {1,…,n} and Xn​=nYn​​. Show Xn​d​U(0,1).

Solution

Solution. For 0≤x≤1, FXn​​(x)=P(Yn​≤nx)=n⌊nx⌋​, and nx−1<⌊nx⌋≤nx gives x−n1​<FXn​​(x)≤x. So FXn​​(x)→x. (Outside [0,1] both CDFs are 0 or 1.)

B19 (probabilitycourse 7.2.8, Problem 1). Xn​∼ Geometric(nλ​) and Yn​=nXn​​. Show Yn​d​ Exp(λ).

Solution

Solution. P(Yn​>y)=P(Xn​>ny)=(1−nλ​)⌊ny⌋→e−λy, because ⌊ny⌋=ny−θ with 0≤θ<1, and (1−nλ​)ny→e−λy while (1−nλ​)−θ→1. (The waiting time in many tiny trials becomes exponential: the continuous analogue of Binomial → Poisson.)

B20 (last year's HW8 Q9): hypergeometric to binomial. A bag has n blue and n red balls; draw 10 without replacement; Xn​ is the number of blue balls. Show Xn​d​ Binomial(10,21​).

Solution

Solution. For k=0,…,10:

P(Xn​=k)=(102n​)(kn​)(10−kn​)​=(k10​)10 factors2n(2n−1)⋯(2n−9)​​n(n−1)⋯(n−k+1)​k factors​⋅n(n−1)⋯(n−9+k)​10−k factors​​ ⟶ (k10​)(2n)10n10​=(k10​)2101​.

By Theorem 7.1 this is convergence in distribution. (Drawing 10 from a huge bag is almost like drawing with replacement.)

B21 (last year's HW8 Q6). Xn​=n​Z​ with E[Z2]<∞. Show Xn​d​0.

Solution

Solution. E[Xn2​]=nE[Z2]​→0, so Xn​→0 in mean square, hence in probability, hence in distribution.

Normal approximation (CLT)

B22 (Bertsekas Ex. 5.9). 100 packages with weights i.i.d. U[5,50] pounds. P(total>3000)?

Solution

Solution. μ=27.5, σ2=12452​=168.75. z=16875​3000−2750​=129.9250​=1.92. P≈1−Φ(1.92)=0.027.

B23 (Bertsekas Ex. 5.10): turning a count into a sum. Processing times are i.i.d. U[1,5]. Find P(at least 100 parts processed within 320 time units).

Solution

Solution. "At least 100 parts by time 320" is the same event as "the first 100 parts take at most 320", {S100​≤320}. μ=3, σ2=1216​=34​. z=100⋅4/3​320−300​=1.73, so P≈Φ(1.73)=0.958.

B24 (Bertsekas Ex. 5.11): polling, revisited. With Mn​ the sample fraction, Var(Mn​)=np(1−p)​≤4n1​, so

P(∣Mn​−p∣≥ϵ)≈2(1−Φ(σMn​​ϵ​))≤2(1−Φ(2ϵn​)).

(a) n=100, ϵ=0.1: ≤2(1−Φ(2))=0.0455 (Chebyshev only gave 0.25). (b) 95% confidence of ±0.01: need 2ϵn​=0.02n​≥1.96, so n≥9604, compared with Chebyshev's 50,000.

B25 (last year's HW8 Q2). Call durations have μ=10 and σ=10 minutes. (a) For 50 calls, P(Xˉ>12). (b) Minimum n with P(Xˉ>12)≤0.05. (c) For 80 calls, P(9<Xˉ<11). (Given: Φ−1(0.95)=1.6449, Φ(2​)=0.9214, Φ(0.8944)=0.8147.)

Solution

Solution. (a) SD(Xˉ)=50​10​, z=10250​​=2​: P≈1−0.9214=0.0786. (b) Need 102n​​≥1.6449, so n​≥8.22 and n≥67.6: n=68. (c) z=10/80​1​=0.8944: P≈2(0.8147)−1=0.6294.

B26 (last year's HW8 Q3). Rods: μ=100 mm, σ=5 mm, roughly normal. (a) P(one rod>110). (b) P(mean of 36>103).

Solution

Solution. (a) z=2: 1−0.9772=0.0228. (b) SD(Xˉ)=65​, z=5/63​=3.6: 1−0.9998=0.0002. Averages vary far less than individuals.

B27 (last year's HW8 Q8 = Bertsekas Problem 8; Tutorial 8 Q8). (a) A fair roulette (odd with probability 21​) is watched for 100 rounds; you call it unfair if more than 55 are odd. P(wrong decision)? (b) P(>220 heads in 400 tosses). Are (a) and (b) the same? (c) P(40≤ heads ≤60) in 100 tosses.

Solution

Solution. (a) S∼ Binomial(100,21​), mean 50, SD 5. "More than 55" is S≥56, so the corrected boundary is 55.5: 1−Φ(1.1)=0.1357 (exact 0.1356; without the correction 1−Φ(1)=0.159). (b) Mean 200, SD 10: 1−Φ(10220.5−200​)=1−Φ(2.05)=0.0202 (exact 0.0201). Not the same, although 55% of 100 equals 55% of 400. The SD of the proportion is n​0.5​, which halves when n quadruples, so the same excess proportion is twice as many standard deviations away. More data makes the same deviation less likely (the LLN at work). (c) P(39.5≤S≤60.5)≈2Φ(2.1)−1=0.9643 (exact 0.9648).

B28 (last year's Tutorial 8 Q6). Test scores: mean 75, SD 10, roughly normal. (a) P(score≥100). (b) Out of 100 people, how many expected below 60? (c) P(mean of 100<70).

Solution

Solution. (a) 1−Φ(2.5)=0.0062. (b) 100⋅Φ(−1.5)=100×0.0668≈6.7 people. (c) SD(Xˉ)=1, so z=−5: Φ(−5)≈2.9×10−7. Essentially impossible.

B29 (last year's Tutorial 8 Q9; probabilitycourse 7.1.2). Service times: mean 2, variance 1, independent. Y = total for 50 customers. P(90<Y<110)?

Solution

Solution. E[Y]=100, SD(Y)=50​. P≈Φ(50​10​)−Φ(−50​10​)=2Φ(2​)−1=0.8427.

B30 (probabilitycourse 7.1.3, Problems 1 to 4).

  1. Plane: 100 passengers, weight mean 170 and SD 30 lb. P(total>18,000): mean 17,000, SD 300, z=310​, so 1−Φ(3.33)≈4.3×10−4.
  2. ±1 steps: Xi​=+1 w.p. 0.6 and −1 w.p. 0.4; Y=X1​+⋯+X25​; estimate P(4≤Y≤6) with a continuity correction. E[Xi​]=0.2 and Var(Xi​)=1−0.04=0.96, so E[Y]=5 and Var(Y)=24. The source's answer uses [3.5,6.5]: 2Φ(24​1.5​)−1=0.2405. A warning worth noticing. A sum of 25 terms equal to ±1 is always odd, so {4≤Y≤6}={Y=5}, with exact probability (1525​)0.6150.410=0.161. The values of Y are 2 apart, so the right correction is half the step, ±1: P(4≤Y≤6)≈2Φ(24​1​)−1=0.162, which is almost exact. The ±21​ rule assumes values 1 apart.
  3. Sandwiches: 64 guests each want 0, 1, 2 sandwiches w.p. 41​,21​,41​. Mean 1, variance 21​ each, so the total has mean 64 and SD 42​=5.66. For 95% confidence, 64+1.6449×5.66=73.3, so make 74.
  4. Sample size: Xi​∼ Exp(1); smallest n with P(0.9≤Xˉ≤1.1)≥0.95. Need 2Φ(0.1n​)−1≥0.95, so 0.1n​≥1.96 and n≥385.

B31 (Bertsekas Problem 9): normal versus Poisson approximation. Each day the computer crashes with probability 0.05, independently. Find P(at least 45 crash-free days out of 50) (a) by the normal approximation, (b) by the Poisson approximation.

Solution

Solution. Let X∼ Binomial(50,0.05) be the number of crash days; we want P(X≤5). Mean 2.5, variance 2.375. (a) Φ(2.375​5.5−2.5​)=Φ(1.95)=0.974. (b) Poisson(2.5): ∑k=05​e−2.5k!2.5k​=0.958. The exact value is 0.962. Poisson wins here because p is small and np is moderate; the binomial is too skewed for the normal approximation.

B32 (Bertsekas Problem 10). Daily gadget counts are i.i.d. with mean 5 and variance 9. (a) P(total in 100 days<440). (b) Largest n with P(X1​+⋯+Xn​≥200+5n)≤0.05. (c) N = first day the total exceeds 1000. Approximate P(N≥220).

Solution

Solution. (a) Mean 500, SD 30: Φ(30440−500​)=Φ(−2)=0.023. (b) P≈1−Φ(3n​200​)≤0.05 requires 3n​200​≥1.645, so n​≤40.5 and n≤1642. (c) N≥220 means the total after 219 days is still at most 1000: P(S219​≤1000)≈Φ(3219​1000−1095​)=Φ(−2.14)=0.016. (Same trick as B23.)

B33 (Bertsekas Problem 11). Xi​,Yi​ i.i.d. U[0,1] and W=16(X1​+⋯+X16​)−(Y1​+⋯+Y16​)​. Approximate P(∣W−E[W]∣<0.001).

Solution

Solution. E[W]=0 and Var(W)=25632⋅121​​=961​, so SD(W)=0.102. P≈2Φ(0.1020.001​)−1=2Φ(0.0098)−1≈0.0078.

B34 (last year's HW8 Q12, bonus): binomial to normal without MGFs (sketch). Write P(k)=(kN​)pkqN−k, take logs, and use Stirling, lnN!≈NlnN−N. With k=Np+x, expand lnP(k) to second order in x around the peak k=Np: the first-order term vanishes (that is why the peak is at Np), and the second-order coefficient is −2Npq1​. So P(k)≈Ce−x2/(2Npq), a Gaussian with mean Np and variance Npq; normalising fixes C=2πNpq​1​. (The finer Stirling formula N!≈2πN​(N/e)N gives the constant directly.)
